opening: A road network, and the question of which single closures would cut it in two.

steps.prompt: Seven towns and eight roads, numbered in this order: road 1 joins towns 1-2, road 2 joins 2-3, road 3 joins 3-1, road 4 joins 3-4, road 5 joins 4-5, road 6 joins 5-6, road 7 joins 6-4, road 8 joins 6-7. Call a road critical if closing it alone leaves some town unreachable from another. Which roads are critical? Give their numbers.
nudges: Close road 1. Can you still get from town 1 to town 2?
Which roads have no detour around them?
steps.showed: Roads 4 and 8. Every other road has a way round.

steps.prompt: A road lies on a cycle of roads. Can it be critical?
options: No: the rest of the cycle is a detour between its two ends
Yes, if the cycle is long
Only if it is the last road of the cycle
nudges: If the road from $a$ to $b$ is closed, how else does the cycle connect $a$ and $b$?
steps.showed: On a cycle means never critical.

steps.prompt: A road lies on no cycle at all. Is it critical?
options: Yes: any other route between its ends would form a cycle together with it
It depends on the rest of the map
nudges: Suppose closing it left its two ends connected. What would that other route and the road make together?
steps.showed: So critical means exactly: on no cycle. The question is how to find these roads without trying each closure.

steps.prompt: Explore from town 1 depth-first: from each town, try its roads in order of road number, and walk a road only if it leads to a town not yet visited. The roads you walk form a tree. Which road numbers were never walked?
nudges: From town 3, where does road 3 lead, and has that town been visited?
steps.showed: Roads 3 and 7: each leads back to a town already visited.

steps.prompt: In a depth-first exploration of a two-way road map, a road that was not walked always joins a town to:
options: one of its own ancestors in the tree of walked roads
a town in a different branch of the tree
nudges: If it led into a different, finished branch, why would that branch not have walked it first?
steps.showed: Unwalked roads only go straight up the tree. This is what makes the next step work.

steps.prompt: A walked road goes from town $p$ down to its child $v$. It is critical exactly when:
options: no unwalked road leads from $v$ or anything below $v$ to $p$ or anything above $p$
nudges: Close the road. What is the only way the part below it could still be attached to the rest?
steps.showed: The subtree of $v$ either has its own way up past the road, or hangs by that road alone.

steps.prompt: Number the towns in the order they were first visited (here that is just 1 to 7). For a town $v$, let low($v$) be the smallest number you can reach from $v$ or anything below it in the tree by using at most one unwalked road. What is low(5)?
nudges: Which towns are below 5 in the tree, and which unwalked road starts among them?
steps.showed: Below 5 are 6 and 7, and road 7 leads from 6 up to 4.

nudges: Does any unwalked road touch town 7?
steps.showed: Town 7 can reach nothing but itself. Its parent is 6, and low(7) = 7 is larger than 6: so the road from 6 to 7 is critical. For town 5, low(5) = 4 is not larger than its parent 4, so that road is safe.

steps.prompt: A different map: five towns joined in a ring, and from one of them a tail of three more towns in a line. How many critical roads does it have?
nudges: Which roads lie on a cycle?
steps.showed: The three tail roads. The five ring roads protect each other.

steps.prompt: A connected graph is explored depth-first, giving a tree of walked edges. Let the tree edge $e$ join $p$ to its child $v$, and let $S$ be the set of $v$ and all its descendants. Prove that removing $e$ disconnects the graph exactly when no other edge has one end in $S$ and the other outside $S$.
claims: Without e, the tree edges inside S still connect all of S, and the remaining tree edges still connect everything outside S.
So after removing e the graph is connected exactly when some remaining edge joins S to the outside.

The only tree edge between S and the outside is e itself, so such an edge would have to be a non-tree edge with one end in S and one outside; if there is none, S is cut off, and if there is one, the two parts are joined.
nudges: After removing $e$, is $S$ still connected within itself? Is the rest?
What would it take to join the two parts again?
steps.showed: Two connected pieces, and the only question is whether anything else links them.

reveal.name: Bridges
reveal.statement: An edge is a bridge (its removal disconnects the graph) exactly when it lies on no cycle. With DFS entry times tin and low($v$) = the smallest tin reachable from the subtree of $v$ by at most one non-tree edge, the tree edge $p \to v$ is a bridge exactly when low($v$) > tin($p$).
reveal.remark: One DFS, $O(n + m)$. Contracting everything that is not a bridge turns any graph into a tree, which is how "edges every path must use" questions are usually answered.
